power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Social media use is increasingly suspected of harming attention, but the evidence remains too limited to draw any firm conclusions.
One obstacle is the lack of a framework specifying how such use might affect attention afterwards, without any device.
To address this gap, we draw on emotional attention, the affective mechanism that prioritises what matters to individuals.
The Relevance Rate Model rests on the relevance rate, the frequency with which an environment delivers concern-relevant stimuli.
Drawing on predictive coding, we suggest that social media raises the rate that users expect, and that this expectation may persist after each session and, with repeated use, across daily life.
When an activity delivers less concern-relevant information than expected, sustained attention to the ongoing task may be disrupted as emotional attention is recruited to address the shortfall.
The model specifies four measurable parameters of use, from which we derive a research agenda.
The growing use of social media over the past decade has become a major societal issue, particularly among adolescents and young adults 1 .
text.formatted: The growing use of social media over the past decade has become a major societal issue, particularly among adolescents and young adults <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">1</ref> .

text.text: Questions have been raised regarding the links between social media use and various psychological, educational, and developmental outcomes, including psychological distress, academic performance and developmental trajectories 2 .
text.formatted: Questions have been raised regarding the links between social media use and various psychological, educational, and developmental outcomes, including psychological distress, academic performance and developmental trajectories <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2</ref> .

text.text: Restrictive policies are thus being implemented even as the consequences of this use remain a subject of debate 3 .
text.formatted: Restrictive policies are thus being implemented even as the consequences of this use remain a subject of debate <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3</ref> .

text.text: Attention plays a central role in this debate, given its importance for daily functioning and mental health 4 .
text.formatted: Attention plays a central role in this debate, given its importance for daily functioning and mental health <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4</ref> .

text.text: Social media cues are well known to capture attention, with notifications diverting resources from the task at hand while they are present 5 .
text.formatted: Social media cues are well known to capture attention, with notifications diverting resources from the task at hand while they are present <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">5</ref> .

text.text: Whether social media use also impairs attention once use has ended, when no cue is present, is less clear.
Despite widespread belief in such a persistent effect, current evidence is too limited to settle the question 6 .
text.formatted: Despite widespread belief in such a persistent effect, current evidence is too limited to settle the question <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">6</ref> .

text.text: In the broader digital media literature, associations with attention are similarly weak and inconsistent 7, 8 , partly for lack of a mechanistic framework specifying which properties of exposure affect which attentional processes 6, 9.
text.formatted: In the broader digital media literature, associations with attention are similarly weak and inconsistent <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">7,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">8</ref> , partly for lack of a mechanistic framework specifying which properties of exposure affect which attentional processes <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">6,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">9</ref>.

text.text: Regarding usage, the evidence linking social media use to attention remains difficult to interpret, largely because of how use is measured.
When participants estimate their cumulative time of use, results are mixed 10, 11 , partly because such estimates correlate only moderately with logged use 12 .
text.formatted: When participants estimate their cumulative time of use, results are mixed <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">10,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">11</ref> , partly because such estimates correlate only moderately with logged use <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">12</ref> .

text.text: Logging cumulative time objectively addresses this issue, yet its links with attention remain small and not always in the expected direction 13, 14 , possibly because the same total can conceal very different patterns of use 15 .
text.formatted: Logging cumulative time objectively addresses this issue, yet its links with attention remain small and not always in the expected direction <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">13,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">14</ref> , possibly because the same total can conceal very different patterns of use <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">15</ref> .

text.text: Studies that distinguished such patterns have reported effects tied to several candidate parameters.
Exposure to dense or rapidly updated content disrupts attention after use [16] [17] [18] [19] [20] [21] .
text.formatted: Exposure to dense or rapidly updated content disrupts attention after use <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[16]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[17]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">[18]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[19]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">[21]</ref> .

text.text: Attentional effects vary from moment to moment, and in strength across individuals, as a function of session length and fragmentation, that is, with how use is distributed across the day [22] [23] [24] .
text.formatted: Attentional effects vary from moment to moment, and in strength across individuals, as a function of session length and fragmentation, that is, with how use is distributed across the day <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[22]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">[23]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">[24]</ref> .

text.text: Finally, effects observed after a reduction or interruption of use, or after weeks of assigned use, suggest that chronic use may produce more persistent changes 14, 25, 26 .
text.formatted: Finally, effects observed after a reduction or interruption of use, or after weeks of assigned use, suggest that chronic use may produce more persistent changes <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">14,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">25,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">26</ref> .

text.text: Whether social media use affects attention may thus depend less on its total duration than on what it delivers and how it unfolds over hours and days.

With regard to attention, these studies have examined several processes, including inattention symptoms 10, 11 , sustained attention 14, 19, 25, 26 , momentary distraction 22 , the monitoring of delayed intentions 18 , inhibitory and proactive control 17, 23, 24 , and the prefrontal activity and frontoparietal connectivity that support it 20, 21 .
text.formatted: With regard to attention, these studies have examined several processes, including inattention symptoms <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">10,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">11</ref> , sustained attention <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">14,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">19,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">25,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">26</ref> , momentary distraction <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">22</ref> , the monitoring of delayed intentions <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">18</ref> , inhibitory and proactive control <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">17,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">23,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">24</ref> , and the prefrontal activity and frontoparietal connectivity that support it <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">20,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">21</ref> .

text.text: Although distinct, each can be read as a failure to keep limited resources on the ongoing activity, and thus as a diversion of endogenous attention, which voluntarily sustains that activity, whether reading a text or following a train of thought 27.
text.formatted: Although distinct, each can be read as a failure to keep limited resources on the ongoing activity, and thus as a diversion of endogenous attention, which voluntarily sustains that activity, whether reading a text or following a train of thought <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">27</ref>.

text.text: Existing frameworks explain several aspects of digital media use, from the costs of media multitasking 8, 28 to reward-driven engagement 29, 30 , online vigilance 31, 32 and effort recalibration 33 (Box 1).

text.text: None, however, aims to explain what diverts endogenous attention once use has ended, nor how the properties of exposure would shape this diversion across timescales.
To answer these two questions, we develop the Relevance Rate Model (RRM), grounded in affectivism, an approach that places affect at the heart of cognition 37 .

It focuses on concern-relevance, defined as the probability that a stimulus will satisfy or dissatisfy a major concern of the organism 38 , such as its needs, goals, values or social standing 39 .

text.text: News of a conflict or of climate obstructs concerns as surely as a like promotes them, and negativity even drives the consumption of online news 41 .

text.text: We therefore propose to characterise exposure by the rate at which concern-relevant stimuli are encountered, whether conducive or obstructive, which we term the relevance rate.
With regard to attention, this framework draws on appraisal theories, according to which emotion arises from the ongoing appraisal of what events mean for the individual 43, 44 .
text.formatted: With regard to attention, this framework draws on appraisal theories, according to which emotion arises from the ongoing appraisal of what events mean for the individual <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">43,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">44</ref> .

text.text: Concern-relevant stimuli are automatically given attentional priority, in order to allocate resources to assessing their consequences and the appropriate response 45 .
text.formatted: Concern-relevant stimuli are automatically given attentional priority, in order to allocate resources to assessing their consequences and the appropriate response <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">45</ref> .

text.text: This mechanism is termed emotional attention 46 .
text.formatted: This mechanism is termed emotional attention <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">46</ref> .

text.text: Whereas endogenous attention is guided by current task goals 27 , emotional attention prioritises concern-relevant stimuli whether or not they serve the task at hand 47 .
text.formatted: Whereas endogenous attention is guided by current task goals <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">27</ref> , emotional attention prioritises concern-relevant stimuli whether or not they serve the task at hand <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">47</ref> .

text.text: The two rely on partially dissociable neural systems, the dorsal frontoparietal network for endogenous attention and the amygdala for emotional attention [48] [49] [50] .

text.text: Yet both bias the competition for the same limited processing capacity, so that concern-relevant stimuli can draw away the resources needed to pursue current goals 51, 52 .
text.formatted: Yet both bias the competition for the same limited processing capacity, so that concern-relevant stimuli can draw away the resources needed to pursue current goals <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">51,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">52</ref> .

text.text: Emotional attention can also be triggered by internal stimuli, such as thoughts 53, 54 , making it a natural candidate for diverting endogenous attention after use, in the absence of an external signal.

text.text: To explain how usage would bring about this diversion, the RRM proposes that the brain learns the relevance rate of its environment, just as it learns other regularities through predictive coding 55 .
text.formatted: To explain how usage would bring about this diversion, the RRM proposes that the brain learns the relevance rate of its environment, just as it learns other regularities through predictive coding <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">55</ref> .

text.text: Exposure to a high relevance rate would thus increase the rate at which the brain expects to encounter concern-relevant stimuli (Fig. 1).
text.formatted: Exposure to a high relevance rate would thus increase the rate at which the brain expects to encounter concern-relevant stimuli (Fig. <ref type="figure">1</ref>).

text.text: When a subsequent activity, such as reading, delivers fewer such stimuli than expected, the resulting relevance-rate mismatch would itself become concern-obstructive, so that concern-relevance comes into play twice, in the stimuli that shape the expectation and in the mismatch that frustrates it.
Its appraisal would recruit emotional attention, diverting resources from the endogenous attention that sustains the activity, even without any social media cue.
We ground each step of the RRM in evidence, examine how patterns of use and individual differences shape it, and derive a research agenda to test it.
Fig. 1 The Relevance Rate Model as a treadmill: upward calibration of an expected relevance rate and its offline consequences.
text.formatted: Fig. <ref type="figure">1</ref> The Relevance Rate Model as a treadmill: upward calibration of an expected relevance rate and its offline consequences.

text.text: Throughout, the belt speed represents the rate at which the environment delivers concern-relevant stimuli (received rate), read on the treadmill console, whereas the pace at which the brain runs represents the internal expectation of that rate (expected relevance rate).
Baseline: in ordinary environments, expected and received rates coincide and the pace is sustainable.
Exposure: social media streams accelerate the belt, delivering concern-relevant items, conducive or obstructive, faster, more personally and with fewer interruptions than most offline settings.
Calibration: the expectation is revised upwards until it matches this higher rate; the pace that was demanding becomes the norm.
Mismatch: on leaving the stream, the belt returns to its ordinary pace while the expectation remains elevated, so the expected rate now exceeds the received rate.
Resolution: this mismatch admits two routes.

Downward recalibration returns the expectation towards the ambient rate and restores baseline, whereas the active route restores the received rate instead, by seeking a higher-rate stream, which re-exposes the user and reinstates the elevated expectation.
With a sustained pattern of use, recalibration returns the expectation only to a raised habitual level.
The pace stands for an expectation, not for attention itself.
Resolving the mismatch is costly because its appraisal recruits emotional attention, which draws on the limited capacity that endogenous attention needs to sustain an ongoing task.

This section examines the four steps of the mechanism: social media delivers concernrelevant stimuli at a high rate, exposure calibrates the expected rate, this expectation persists after use, and the resulting mismatch recruits emotional attention (Fig. 1).

text.text: In the RRM, it is a distinct source of attentional control that shares limited capacity with emotional attention.
The rate at which an environment delivers stimuli appraised as concern-relevant.
It is a property of the environment, which depends on how often new items arrive and on the likelihood that they bear on the individual's concerns.
Expected relevance rate.
The internal expectation, learned from exposure, of how often concern-relevant stimuli are likely to arrive.
It is revised on two timescales.

It rises quickly during use and falls back gradually afterwards, towards a resting level, the habitual expectation, which reflects daily life as a whole and shifts more slowly with the pattern of use.
Persistence.
The carryover of an elevated expectation beyond use.
It takes two forms, the after-effect of a session, which fades within minutes to hours after use, and a raised habitual expectation, which a sustained pattern of use maintains over days.
The inverse of the variance of a signal or of a prediction.
In predictive coding, the precision of an incoming signal relative to that of the prediction sets how strongly a prediction error revises a belief.
Relevance-rate mismatch.
The shortfall of the rate an activity delivers below the expectation carried into it.
Because a rate is estimated over time, it accumulates from intervals with few concern-relevant events as much as from those that deliver them.
Although concern-obstructive, it is a signal about the rate rather than an event the activity delivers, and so does not enter the rate it measures.

text.text: Whether active or passive, usage thus exposes the user to a succession of content that may relate to their concerns.

text.text: The implications of each piece of content for the user must therefore be appraised, which is precisely the role of emotional attention.

text.text: Other environments also deliver concernrelevant stimuli, from work and relationships to a gripping novel or a binge-watched series, but rarely combine this density, personalisation and ease of access.
A high relevance rate can affect subsequent attention only if the brain learns this regularity and the resulting expectation outlasts use.
For the first condition, calibration, predictive coding offers a general mechanism.
The brain does not simply react to incoming events but anticipates them, deriving expectations from regularities in past input and registering departures from those expectations 55 .
text.formatted: The brain does not simply react to incoming events but anticipates them, deriving expectations from regularities in past input and registering departures from those expectations <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">55</ref> .

text.text: Regularities in an event stream can be learned incidentally, without intention or awareness 62 , and expectations about upcoming events, including their timing, are updated as the statistics of the environment change 63 .

text.text: Expectations about when events will occur can, in turn, guide the temporal allocation of attention 64 .

text.text: The RRM extends this general learning capacity to the frequency of events appraised as concern-relevant.
Repeated exposure to a high relevance rate may therefore calibrate an expectation about how frequently such events are likely to occur.
We propose that this calibration is fast.
An expectation formed in a calm activity predicts few concern-relevant events, with little variation around that number.
A dense stream delivers many more from its first minutes, which signals that the environment has changed rather than fluctuated, a condition under which expectations are revised faster 63.

text.text: Extending these findings to concern-relevance, we propose that exposure to a high relevance rate raises the expected rate against which the amygdala evaluates incoming events.
Persistence is the second condition.
Leaving the stream also signals a change in environment, which should speed the downward revision, yet expectations about concern-relevant events appear to resist it.

text.text: Evidence suggests that persistence operates on two timescales.
The first, shortterm, follows each session: distraction fluctuates from hour to hour with the fragmentation of use 22 .

text.text: To account for this, the RRM proposes that, following a session, the expectation falls back within minutes to hours.
This constitutes the session's after-effect.
However, it does not drop back to a fixed baseline, but rather to a resting level, the habitual expectation, which reflects the rate delivered by daily life as a whole.

This resting level rises slowly with each session that maintains the expectation above it, so that after several days of repeated use, a mismatch may arise in the absence of a recent session, and this level only returns to normal when the usage pattern changes.

text.text: The expected relevance rate, however, is abstract, as users anticipate only that concern-relevant information arrives at roughly a certain rate, not what it will be.

text.text: Here, the shared structure, events relating to concerns that occur at a certain rate, is common to all activities, so that the transfer requires no social-media-related cues.
What persists is therefore an expectation, not an attentional state.
During use, emotional attention is engaged by the content itself, with no ongoing task to disrupt.
After use, only the elevated expectation remains, and endogenous attention would be diverted only when a subsequent task delivers less than this expectation predicts.
Persistence gives rise to a relevance-rate mismatch when the expectation brought into an activity exceeds the rate that activity delivers.
It could stem from either form of persistence, though more strongly from the after-effect than from a raised habitual expectation.
In both cases, the mismatch is greatest when the subsequent activity is calm.
In terms of predictive coding, the mismatch is a prediction error 55 .

Each posterior becomes the prior for the next interval, so that as long as the prior remains above what the activity yields, the shortfall recurs.
The mismatch is therefore not a single event but a prediction error that persists throughout the activity (Fig. 2).

text.text: The RRM focuses instead on the competition that precedes this choice.
At the start of a task, the goal of performing it dominates, and endogenous attention sustains it.
As the shortfall gains precision, the concern it obstructs would gain weight relative to this goal, until it recruits emotional attention.
Resources would then go to appraising the shortfall, its consequences and the response it calls for.
Because emotional and endogenous attention compete for the same limited capacity 51, 52 , these resources would be withdrawn from the ongoing task, whichever route is eventually taken.

text.text: As this shift occurs when one goal overtakes the other, it should produce intermittent lapses rather than a steady decline in performance.
This mechanism offers a common reading of reported effects.
Without competing stimuli, the diversion would appear as momentary distraction, inattention, reduced sustained attention or failures to monitor intentions 10, [17] [18] [19] 25 .

text.text: The studies reviewed in the introduction point to four candidate parameters of use, namely the within-session relevance rate, which combines the density and concernrelevance of the feed [16] [17] [18] [19] [20] [21] ; the duration and fragmentation of sessions [22] [23] [24] ; and the chronicity of usage 14, 25, 26 .

text.text: When these parameters are studied separately, their interactions may be overlooked.
The RRM integrates them as a leaky bucket, which each session fills and which empties between sessions down to a resting level, the habitual expectation, itself rising with sustained use.
The within-session relevance rate sets the level the expectation approaches during use.
It depends on both the rate at which new content arrives and its relevance to the user's concerns, although how the two combine over the course of a session remains to be established.
Speed is increased by continuous feeds and short-form content 42 , as well as by the users themselves, through rapid scrolling, skipping or fast-forwarding 85 .
text.formatted: Speed is increased by continuous feeds and short-form content 42 , as well as by the users themselves, through rapid scrolling, skipping or fast-forwarding <ref type="bibr" target="#b84">85</ref> .

text.text: Concern-relevance is enhanced by recommendation systems, which personalise content based on past engagement 42 .
text.formatted: Concern-relevance is enhanced by recommendation systems, which personalise content based on past engagement <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">42</ref> .

text.text: Session duration and fragmentation are two sides of the same coin.
Because calibration is fast, duration should matter only until the expectation reaches the rate of the stream.
Fragmentation then takes over, since a return maintains the expectation only if it comes before the expectation has subsided, so that the spacing of sessions matters more than their number.
For the same total duration, fragmented use would therefore keep the expectation elevated for longer than a single long session (Fig. 3).
text.formatted: For the same total duration, fragmented use would therefore keep the expectation elevated for longer than a single long session (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">3</ref>).

text.text: Chronicity operates on a slow timescale.
Each session that keeps the expectation above the habitual level raises that level slightly.
For the same usage pattern, a user who has maintained it for a week rather than a day therefore returns to a higher resting level between sessions.  2.

text.text: After their morning session (10:00), both users carry the same elevated expectation, because it reaches the stream's rate early in a session.
By 16:00, it has returned to its resting level for the concentrated user, whilst the fragmented user's final session has reinstated it.
For the same total duration, fragmentation thus prolongs the mismatch throughout the day.

This view also exposes the limits of current usage metrics.
Cumulative time adds up sessions regardless of their distribution, although the level of the bucket may differ for the same total (Fig. 3).

text.text: Questionnaires derived from existing frameworks (Box 1) measure simultaneous use, problematic use or online vigilance rather than the parameters that calibrate the expectation.
They also rely on self-report, which diverges from logged behaviour 12.

text.text: Individual differences and transient states may increase vulnerability by making an elevated expected relevance rate more likely to be reached, maintained or acted upon.

Boredom proneness 85 , need to belong 86 , anxiety 87 and FoMO 88 may raise the withinsession relevance rate, by increasing scrolling speed and the likelihood that content bears on the user's concerns.

text.text: Because expectations about concern-relevant events resist downward revision, the same dispositions may also lengthen the after-effect, thus acting twice.
Others may increase between-session fragmentation by raising the likelihood of picking up the phone.

Momentary fatigue 89 and emotion-regulation difficulties 90 may do so by making the current state harder to tolerate, and attention-deficit traits 4 by making it harder to stay with a task other than the phone.

text.text: Adolescence may displace several parameters at once.
Peer approval and social evaluation become dominant concerns, raising the expected concern-relevance of social streams 91 and making the expectation resist downward revision once the stream is left.

text.text: Fragmentation may also increase, as still-developing sustained attention 92 favours returning to the stream over holding a task, and younger users indeed show more fragmented smartphone use 93 .

text.text: Calibration may in turn be faster, since adolescents learn from social feedback at a higher rate than adults 94 .

text.text: Faster learning would also speed the decay of the expectation after use, but with frequent returns to the stream, it should mainly serve calibration, each new session quickly bringing the expectation back up.
These influences therefore converge on greater exposure, making adolescence, and the early adulthood into which these changes extend 95 , a period of heightened vulnerability.

text.text: Later adulthood may also carry vulnerability.
Isolation becomes more likely at this age 96 , and unmet belonging needs heighten the monitoring of social cues 86 , which may raise the expected concern-relevance of social streams.

text.text: The questions this literature has to address are whether social media use leaves attention impaired once a session has ended, and whether that impairment persists.
The RRM makes both questions answerable by turning them into two quantities.
The first is the after-effect, the elevated expectation that follows a session and falls back within minutes to hours.
The second is the habitual expectation towards which it falls back, built up over days of repeated use and declining over days once use stops.
In both cases, sustained attention and attentional lapses may be measured with tasks that are well established 19, 25, 26 , scored for moment-to-moment stability rather than mean performance 98 .

text.text: What changes is when they are administered, after a fixed period of use, say ten minutes, or after a fixed period of full abstinence as used in restriction studies 25 .

text.text: The model also predicts when the cost should be greatest.
A session taken as a break from a calm task, such as studying, should disrupt attention on returning to that task more than a session followed by a denser activity.
Conversely, the more the ongoing task matters, through stakes or deadlines, the later the shortfall should overtake the goal of performing it, and the later lapses should appear.

Administered in the scanner, these tasks would show whether windows of unstable performance coincide with amygdala activation, whose connectivity with attention networks already relates to sustained-attention performance 99 .

text.text: Unstable windows without amygdala involvement would qualify the role attributed to emotional attention.
What is most urgently needed, though, is a better measure of use, one that would serve this literature whether or not the mechanism proposed here proves correct.
The four parameters can be derived from scrolling logs and from the times at which sessions start and end, which tracking tools make increasingly feasible to collect 100 .
text.formatted: The four parameters can be derived from scrolling logs and from the times at which sessions start and end, which tracking tools make increasingly feasible to collect <ref type="bibr" target="#b99">100</ref> .

text.text: Only the concern-relevance of content escapes the log, and could be approached through experience sampling.
Future studies could combine these parameters into an exposure index that behaves like the leaky bucket described above, rising during sessions, draining between them and drifting with sustained use.
Its weights and timescales can be estimated, and the index compared against simpler descriptions of use down to cumulative time.
If cumulative time accounts for attention best, the model's central claim is rejected.
Should the model fail, the same comparison would still identify which description of use is best supported, including descriptions the model does not privilege.
What remains open is how far the model extends across individuals.
The dispositions discussed above are starting points rather than predictions.
Age differs, because several parameters move together in a direction the model can specify [92] [93] [94] .

text.text: Two comparisons follow.

Across the patterns of use that individuals actually display, adolescents and young adults should show stronger associations between the expected relevance rate and attentional disruption than older adults.
At matched patterns of use, comparing the after-effect across ages would show whether faster learning from social feedback or the greater concern-relevance of social content dominates.
A shorter aftereffect in younger users would indicate that faster learning dominates.
This prediction matters because age-based restrictions are being implemented despite the absence of supporting experimental evidence 3.

text.text: Whether social media affects attention has been debated for over a decade, and one obstacle has been the lack of an account specifying both the relevant exposure and the mechanism at stake.
The RRM offers one such account.
It proposes that the brain learns the relevance rate of its environment, like other statistical regularities.
Streams that deliver concern-relevant stimuli rapidly and repeatedly may thus calibrate upwards the rate users expect.
When this expectation carries over into activities that deliver a lower rate, the resulting mismatch may recruit emotional attention away from the ongoing task.
Because emotional and endogenous attention are distinct sources of control, this cost depends on their sharing a limited capacity.
If they drew on independent resources, the mismatch would leave the ongoing task intact, which makes attentional disruption after use a direct test of this shared capacity.
The contribution is both theoretical and methodological.
Theoretically, the model identifies one way in which digital environments might affect cognition.
Rather than depleting attentional capacity, they may shift what the brain has learned to expect from its surroundings.
Unlike reward-based accounts, the model counts obstructive events as much as conducive ones.
Methodologically, the model characterises exposure through four parameters that can be computed from logged use, rather than through time spent alone.
In doing so, it turns broad questions about the effects of social media into estimable ones.
Which patterns of use affect attention, over what timescale and for whom?
These questions are worth pursuing whether or not the mechanism proposed here proves to be the right one.
